title: "forgive us as we forgive"
hook: "forgive us as we forgive" — the one clause with a condition in it

segments.voice: Yesterday, line three: give us this day our daily bread. Just today's, and for all of us. Your line was enough for today. Did you notice when there already was enough? Now, line four. Day seven.

Read the fine print. Every contract has it: the little clause that says, this only works if. Now look at the Lord's Prayer. Almost every line is a plain request. Your kingdom come. Give us bread. Deliver us. But one line has a condition built right into it, and it's the line we're on today. Forgive us, as we forgive. It's a strange thing to pray, if you stop and listen. It asks to be forgiven the same way we forgive other people. Which means the person who cut you off, the friend who never paid you back, the sibling who said the thing, all of them just walked into the prayer. Line four of five.
screen: `THE FINE PRINT.` → `ONE LINE WITH A CONDITION.` → `EVERYONE YOU'RE MAD AT, INSIDE.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible, Matthew chapter six, it reads: "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Debts. Money language. Jesus spoke Aramaic, and in Aramaic the same word could mean a debt or a sin: something you owe. So forgiving is like tearing up an IOU. Not collecting. That's why churches say it differently today. Some say debts. Many say trespasses, the word most Anglicans, Catholics and Methodists use, which comes from an early English Bible's wording of the verses just after the prayer. Luke's version says sins. Same idea, three doors into it. Now the Greek verb for forgive. It's aphiemi, and its first meaning is to let go. To release. To send away, the way you'd open your hand and let a bird fly off. Forgiving, in this word, isn't pretending it didn't happen, and many Christians are quick to say it isn't the same as trusting someone again. It's letting go of the debt. And here's the surprise. When Jesus finishes teaching the prayer in Matthew, he goes back and comments on only one line. This one. "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." Out of the whole prayer, that's the part he underlines. Christians have wrestled with it ever since. Most say God's forgiveness is a gift, never a wage, and that a forgiven person becomes someone who forgives. Either way, the two go together. You can't hold your hand open to receive and keep it clenched at the same time. And this is day seven, the end of a week. Amen, grace, Jesus, our Father, the kingdom, bread, and now: let it go.
screen: `DEBTS — TEARING UP THE IOU.` · `APHIEMI — TO LET GO.` · `THE ONE LINE HE UNDERLINES.` · then, large: `AN OPEN HAND.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, make a fist, and think of one small thing someone owes you. Not the biggest wound. Something small. On the second, keep holding it, and notice how tight that feels. On the third, open your hand as you breathe out. If you pray, you can say the line: forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. If you don't, just let the hand stay open.
Line four of the Lord's Prayer. Forgive us as we forgive: let go of the debt, the way you hope yours are let go. Seventh word.
Your line: let something go. One small thing today. The late reply, the dish left in the sink, the comment from last week. Open the hand on just one. Day seven.

howItsDone: Christians pray this line every time they say the Lord's Prayer. Some churches say "debts," many say "trespasses," and some use Luke's "sins"; many Christians also make a habit of naming someone to forgive when they reach this line.

original.note: Greek: forgive, let go — the command form of aphiemi, the word in "forgive us" (Matthew 6:12).

trapdoor: what you thought: saying sorry to God.
what it means: letting go of what's owed, both ways. forgive us, as we forgive.
what a scholar hears: in Aramaic one word could mean a debt or a sin. Matthew kept the money word; Luke wrote sins, then kept the debt in the next half: everyone indebted to us.

notes: Which churches say which word is generalized: 'debts' (many Presbyterian and Reformed churches), 'trespasses' (most Anglicans, Catholics, Methodists, via Tyndale and the Book of Common Prayer), 'sins' (Luke, and some modern texts). Confirm, and confirm the attribution of 'trespasses' to an early English Bible (Tyndale's wording of Matthew 6:14–15).
Aramaic hoba as debt/sin: a common scholarly claim, stated simply. Confirm.

The script says forgiveness is 'not pretending it didn't happen' and 'not the same as trusting someone again'; attributed to 'many Christians'. Keeper may want to check tone for listeners carrying serious harm.

Matthew 6:15 (the negative half: 'if ye forgive not…') is not quoted; the script mentions Christians wrestling with the condition and gives the common grace-first reading as what 'most say'. Confirm fair.
